# Multi-Area OSPF Troubleshooting Lab (v2)

You're the network engineer for a small enterprise WAN running live in GNS3: an edge router with two ISP uplinks, two hub routers, four branch routers, and ten hosts. The network has drifted from its design and users are reporting connectivity problems, but nobody has pinned down what is failing or why. There may be more than one fault, anywhere in the lab. Your job is to find every fault, fix each one at its root, and show that the network matches its design again.

This run is unattended, so nobody will be around to answer questions. When you hit a judgment call, make the call a careful engineer would make and explain it in your report.

## Access

Every device has an out-of-band management interface on 192.168.122.0/24 that you can reach over SSH from this machine. Python 3 and netmiko are available. With 19 devices, a small reusable script is the practical way to run commands across them.

| Device | Platform | Mgmt address | Mgmt interface | netmiko `device_type` | Login |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HQ-Edge | VyOS | 192.168.122.11 | eth3 | `vyos` | vyos / test |
| Hub-A | VyOS | 192.168.122.12 | eth4 | `vyos` | vyos / test |
| Hub-B | VyOS | 192.168.122.13 | eth3 | `vyos` | vyos / test |
| ISP-A | VyOS | 192.168.122.14 | eth3 | `vyos` | vyos / test |
| ISP-B | VyOS | 192.168.122.15 | eth3 | `vyos` | vyos / test |
| Branch-1 | MikroTik RouterOS 7 | 192.168.122.21 | ether4 | `mikrotik_routeros` | admin / test |
| Branch-2 | MikroTik RouterOS 7 | 192.168.122.22 | ether4 | `mikrotik_routeros` | admin / test |
| Branch-3 | MikroTik RouterOS 7 | 192.168.122.23 | ether4 | `mikrotik_routeros` | admin / test |
| Branch-4 | MikroTik RouterOS 7 | 192.168.122.24 | ether4 | `mikrotik_routeros` | admin / test |
| B1-PC1, B1-PC2 | Alpine Linux | 192.168.122.31, .32 | eth3 | `linux` | root / alpine |
| B2-PC1, B2-PC2 | Alpine Linux | 192.168.122.33, .34 | eth3 | `linux` | root / alpine |
| B3-PC1, B3-PC2 | Alpine Linux | 192.168.122.35, .36 | eth3 | `linux` | root / alpine |
| B4-PC1 … B4-PC4 | Alpine Linux | 192.168.122.37 … .40 | eth3 | `linux` | root / alpine |

Hub-A is the exception: its management interface is eth4, and its eth3 is a lab link to Branch-3.

You reach every device through the management plane, and nobody can restore it if it breaks during the run. On every device, leave the management interface, the SSH service and the login accounts exactly as they are. The management network is not part of the lab either. It has no gateway and should never appear in OSPF, and a ping between management addresses tells you nothing about the lab, so always test with lab addresses.

Work from the live devices and this document. Don't search this machine for configuration files, answer keys or notes, because the point is to troubleshoot the network in front of you. Keep any scripts you write in the current directory.

## Topology

```
     ISP-A  lo 8.8.8.8                       ISP-B  lo 1.1.1.1
          \  203.0.113.0/30                 /  203.0.113.4/30
           \                               /
            +---------- HQ-Edge ----------+           ASBR, eBGP + NAT to both ISPs
                           |  172.16.1.0/30                            area 0
                         Hub-A                        ABR 0/10
           +---------------+----------------+
     172.16.10.0/30   172.16.10.4/30   172.16.10.8/30                  area 10
           |               |                |
       Branch-1        Branch-2         Branch-3
      10.1.1.0/24     10.1.2.0/24      10.1.3.0/24
                                            |  172.16.20.0/30          area 10
                                          Hub-B                       ABR 10/20
                                            |  172.16.20.4/30          area 20 (totally stubby)
                                        Branch-4
                                10.2.1.0/24    10.2.2.0/24

        Hub-A <====== virtual link through area 10 ======> Hub-B
```

### Interfaces

| Device | Interface | Address | Connects to | OSPF |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HQ-Edge | eth0 | 172.16.1.1/30 | Hub-A eth0 | area 0 |
| HQ-Edge | eth1 | 203.0.113.2/30 | ISP-A eth0 | not in OSPF (eBGP to ISP-A) |
| HQ-Edge | eth2 | 203.0.113.6/30 | ISP-B eth0 | not in OSPF (eBGP to ISP-B) |
| Hub-A | eth0 | 172.16.1.2/30 | HQ-Edge eth0 | area 0 |
| Hub-A | eth1 | 172.16.10.1/30 | Branch-1 ether1 | area 10 |
| Hub-A | eth2 | 172.16.10.5/30 | Branch-2 ether1 | area 10 |
| Hub-A | eth3 | 172.16.10.9/30 | Branch-3 ether1 | area 10 |
| Hub-B | eth0 | 172.16.20.1/30 | Branch-3 ether3 | area 10 |
| Hub-B | eth1 | 172.16.20.5/30 | Branch-4 ether1 | area 20 |
| Branch-1 | ether1 | 172.16.10.2/30 | Hub-A eth1 | area 10 |
| Branch-1 | ether2 | 10.1.1.1/24 | LAN: B1-PC1, B1-PC2 | area 10, passive |
| Branch-2 | ether1 | 172.16.10.6/30 | Hub-A eth2 | area 10 |
| Branch-2 | ether2 | 10.1.2.1/24 | LAN: B2-PC1, B2-PC2 | area 10, passive |
| Branch-3 | ether1 | 172.16.10.10/30 | Hub-A eth3 | area 10 |
| Branch-3 | ether2 | 10.1.3.1/24 | LAN: B3-PC1, B3-PC2 | area 10, passive |
| Branch-3 | ether3 | 172.16.20.2/30 | Hub-B eth0 | area 10 |
| Branch-4 | ether1 | 172.16.20.6/30 | Hub-B eth1 | area 20 |
| Branch-4 | ether2 | 10.2.1.1/24 | LAN: B4-PC1, B4-PC2 | area 20, passive |
| Branch-4 | ether3 | 10.2.2.1/24 | LAN: B4-PC3, B4-PC4 | area 20, passive |
| ISP-A | eth0 | 203.0.113.1/30 | HQ-Edge eth1 | none |
| ISP-A | lo | 8.8.8.8/32 | test target, advertised in BGP | none |
| ISP-B | eth0 | 203.0.113.5/30 | HQ-Edge eth2 | none |
| ISP-B | lo | 1.1.1.1/32 | test target, advertised in BGP | none |

OSPF router IDs: HQ-Edge 10.255.0.1, Hub-A 10.255.0.2, Hub-B 10.255.0.3, Branch-1 10.255.1.1, Branch-2 10.255.1.2, Branch-3 10.255.1.3, Branch-4 10.255.2.1.

### Hosts

Every host has a static address on eth0 and uses its branch router's LAN address as the default gateway. B4-PC3 and B4-PC4 are on the guest LAN (see Design).

| Host | Address | Gateway | Host | Address | Gateway |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B1-PC1 | 10.1.1.10/24 | 10.1.1.1 | B3-PC2 | 10.1.3.11/24 | 10.1.3.1 |
| B1-PC2 | 10.1.1.11/24 | 10.1.1.1 | B4-PC1 | 10.2.1.10/24 | 10.2.1.1 |
| B2-PC1 | 10.1.2.10/24 | 10.1.2.1 | B4-PC2 | 10.2.1.11/24 | 10.2.1.1 |
| B2-PC2 | 10.1.2.11/24 | 10.1.2.1 | B4-PC3 | 10.2.2.10/24 | 10.2.2.1 |
| B3-PC1 | 10.1.3.10/24 | 10.1.3.1 | B4-PC4 | 10.2.2.11/24 | 10.2.2.1 |

## Design

This section and the tables above are the source of truth. When the live network disagrees with them, the network is wrong. If the design doesn't settle whether something is a fault, leave it alone and mention it in your report.

- **Areas.** All routers except the ISPs run OSPFv2. Area 0 is the HQ-Edge to Hub-A link. Area 10 contains Hub-A's three branch links, Branch-1/2/3 and the Branch-3 to Hub-B link, and Hub-A is its ABR to area 0. Area 20 contains the Hub-B to Branch-4 link and Branch-4's LANs, and Hub-B is its ABR.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a given bash command and returns its output.

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 600000ms / 10 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.
 - When running `find`, search from `.` (or a specific path), not `/` — scanning the full filesystem can exhaust system resources on large trees.
 - When using `find -regex` with alternation, put the longest alternative first. Example: use `'.*\.\(tsx\|ts\)'` not `'.*\.\(ts\|tsx\)'` — the second form silently skips `.tsx` files.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.

- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.

- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

I've collected all the data. Let me analyze the faults I've found:

1. **Hub-A eth0**: MD5 key `LabArea0key` (lowercase k) vs design `LabArea0Key` — breaks area 0 adjacency
2. **Hub-A**: area 10 range 10.1.0.0/**24** instead of /16
3. **Hub-B**: virtual-link peer `172.16.10.9` (an IP) instead of router-ID `10.255.0.2`
4. **HQ-Edge**: local-preference 200 on ISP-B-IN instead of ISP-A-IN — wrong preferred ISP
5. **HQ-Edge**: NAT rule 110 on eth1 instead of eth2 — ISP-B traffic not NATed
6. **HQ-Edge**: `default-information originate always` — "always" not in design
7. **Branch-2**: MTU 1400 on ether1 — causes ExStart with Hub-A (MTU mismatch)
8. **Branch-2**: LAN interface-template missing `passive`
9. **Branch-3**: firewall rule dropping OSPF in forward chain — not in design
10. **Branch-4**: area 20 type `default` instead of `stub` — can't form adjacency with Hub-B
11. **Branch-4**: firewall rule 0 accepts all unconditionally — guest isolation broken, needs connection-state
12. **B1-PC2**: subnet mask /16 instead of /24

Let me fix these one device at a time, starting with Hub-A.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fix Hub-A: MD5 key case, area 10 range mask."""
from netmiko import ConnectHandler
import time

conn = ConnectHandler(host="192.168.122.12", device_type="vyos", username="vyos", password="test")

# Fix 1: MD5 key on eth0 (LabArea0key -> LabArea0Key)
# Fix 2: area 10 range 10.1.0.0/24 -> 10.1.0.0/16
commands = [
    "delete protocols ospf interface eth0 authentication md5 key-id 1",
    "set protocols ospf interface eth0 authentication md5 key-id 1 md5-key 'LabArea0Key'",
    "delete protocols ospf area 10 range 10.1.0.0/24",
    "set protocols ospf area 10 range 10.1.0.0/16",
]

output = conn.send_config_set(commands, exit_config_mode=False)

output = conn.commit()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fix Branch-4: area 20 type -> stub, fix firewall for stateful guest isolation."""
from netmiko import ConnectHandler
import time

conn = ConnectHandler(host="192.168.122.24", device_type="mikrotik_routeros", username="admin", password="test")

# Fix 1: Change area 20 to stub type
out = conn.send_command('/routing ospf area set [find name=area20] type=stub', read_timeout=15)
print("AREA STUB:", out)

# Verify area
out = conn.send_command('/routing ospf area print detail', read_timeout=15)
print("AREA AFTER:", out)

# Fix 2: Fix firewall - need connection tracking on "allow return traffic" rule
# First get ID of current rule 0 (accept all)
out = conn.send_command(':put [/ip firewall filter find comment="allow return traffic"]', read_timeout=15)
print("RULE0 ID:", repr(out))

# Remove all existing firewall rules
out = conn.send_command(':put [/ip firewall filter find]', read_timeout=15)
print("ALL IDs:", repr(out))

# Remove them all and recreate properly
ids = out.strip()
if ids:
    for rule_id in ids.split(';'):
        rule_id = rule_id.strip()
        out = conn.send_command(f'/ip firewall filter remove {rule_id}', read_timeout=15)
        print(f"Removed {rule_id}:", out)

# Recreate with proper stateful rules
out = conn.send_command('/ip firewall filter add chain=forward action=accept connection-state=established,related comment="allow return traffic"', read_timeout=15)
print("ADD rule 1:", out)

out = conn.send_command('/ip firewall filter add chain=forward action=drop src-address=10.2.2.0/24 dst-address=10.0.0.0/8 comment="guest LAN: no access to internal networks"', read_timeout=15)
print("ADD rule 2:", out)

out = conn.send_command('/ip firewall filter add chain=forward action=drop src-address=10.0.0.0/8 dst-address=10.2.2.0/24 comment="guest LAN: no new connections from internal networks"', read_timeout=15)
print("ADD rule 3:", out)

# Verify
out = conn.send_command("/ip firewall filter print terse", read_timeout=15)
print("FIREWALL AFTER:", out)

# Wait for OSPF neighbor
time.sleep(20)
out = conn.send_command("/routing ospf neighbor print detail", read_timeout=15)
print("NEIGHBORS:", out)

out = conn.send_command("/ip route print terse", read_timeout=15)
print("ROUTES:", out)

conn.disconnect()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fix HQ-Edge: BGP local-pref, NAT rule 110, default-info originate."""
from netmiko import ConnectHandler
import time

conn = ConnectHandler(host="192.168.122.11", device_type="vyos", username="vyos", password="test")

commands = [
    # Fix local-preference: move from ISP-B-IN to ISP-A-IN
    "delete policy route-map ISP-B-IN rule 10 set local-preference",
    "set policy route-map ISP-A-IN rule 10 set local-preference 200",
    # Fix NAT rule 110: change outbound from eth1 to eth2
    "set nat source rule 110 outbound-interface name 'eth2'",
    # Fix default-information originate: remove 'always'
    "delete protocols ospf default-information originate always",
    "set protocols ospf default-information originate",
]

output = conn.send_config_set(commands, exit_config_mode=False)
print("CONFIG OUTPUT:", output)

output = conn.commit()
print("COMMIT OUTPUT:", output)

output = conn.send_command_timing("save")
print("SAVE OUTPUT:", output)

output = conn.send_command_timing("exit")
print("EXIT OUTPUT:", output)

# Verify FRR config
time.sleep(5)
frr = conn.send_command("vtysh -c 'show running-config'", read_timeout=30)
print("\nFRR RUNNING CONFIG:")
print(frr)

# Check BGP
time.sleep(5)
bgp = conn.send_command("show ip bgp", read_timeout=30)
print("\nBGP TABLE:")
print(bgp)

# Check config
cfg = conn.send_command("show configuration commands | grep -E 'nat|route-map|default-info'", read_timeout=30)
print("\nRELEVANT CONFIG:")
print(cfg)

# Check NAT rules
nat = conn.send_command("show nat source rules", read_timeout=30)
print("\nNAT RULES:")
print(nat)

conn.disconnect()
PYEOF

content.text: FRR has a bug where `area range` doesn't suppress component Type-3 LSAs. The summary 10.2.0.0/16 is created but the /24s persist. Let me use FRR's area filter-list to suppress them — this is the standard OSPF mechanism for controlling inter-area LSAs.

input.command:
cat << 'PYEOF' > /home/doarte/claudenetops/opus/run_009/fix_hub_b_filter.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fix Hub-B: add area filter-list to suppress /24 component LSAs in area 10."""
from netmiko import ConnectHandler
import time

conn = ConnectHandler(host="192.168.122.13", device_type="vyos", username="vyos", password="test")

# Check if VyOS supports area filter-list
# VyOS uses: set protocols ospf area <N> area-type ...
# But filter-list might need direct vtysh configuration

# Use VyOS configuration 
commands = [
    "set policy prefix-list AREA20-SUMMARY rule 10 action deny",
    "set policy prefix-list AREA20-SUMMARY rule 10 prefix 10.2.0.0/16",
    "set policy prefix-list AREA20-SUMMARY rule 10 ge 17",
    "set policy prefix-list AREA20-SUMMARY rule 20 action permit",
    "set policy prefix-list AREA20-SUMMARY rule 20 prefix 0.0.0.0/0",
    "set policy prefix-list AREA20-SUMMARY rule 20 le 32",
    "set protocols ospf area 10 area-type normal",
]
output = conn.send_config_set(commands, exit_config_mode=False)
print("CONFIG1:", output)

output = conn.commit()
print("COMMIT1:", output)

output = conn.send_command_timing("save")
print("SAVE:", output)
output = conn.send_command_timing("exit")
print("EXIT:", output)

# Now apply the filter-list via vtysh since VyOS may not have a direct mapping
out = conn.send_command("vtysh -c 'conf t' -c 'router ospf' -c 'area 10 filter-list prefix AREA20-SUMMARY in'", read_timeout=15)
print("VTYSH FILTER:", out)

time.sleep(20)

# Check results
out = conn.send_command("vtysh -c 'show running-config'", read_timeout=30)
print("FRR CONFIG:")
print(out)

conn.disconnect()

# Check Branch-1 routes
time.sleep(10)
conn2 = ConnectHandler(host="192.168.122.21", device_type="mikrotik_routeros", username="admin", password="test")
out = conn2.send_command("/ip route print terse where dst-address~\"10.2\"", read_timeout=15)
print("\nBranch-1 10.2 routes:")
print(out)
conn2.disconnect()
PYEOF

Let me also verify the `area-type normal` setting didn't add anything unwanted, and that the filter-list will persist across VyOS reloads.

input.command:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Make the area filter-list persistent in VyOS config."""
from netmiko import ConnectHandler
import time

conn = ConnectHandler(host="192.168.122.13", device_type="vyos", username="vyos", password="test")

# Check if VyOS has the filter-list in its config
out = conn.send_command("show configuration commands | grep filter", read_timeout=15)
print("VyOS filter config:", out)

# If not present, add it via VyOS set commands
# VyOS might use: set protocols ospf area 10 area-filter-list ...
# Let me check what VyOS options are available

# Actually, let me just check all ospf config 
out = conn.send_command("show configuration commands | grep ospf", read_timeout=15)
print("\nVyOS OSPF config:", out)

# The filter-list was added via vtysh, not VyOS. Let me check if VyOS has a mapping.
# VyOS has: set protocols ospf area <N> filter-list ...
# Let me try
commands = [
    "set protocols ospf area 10 filter-list prefix-list 'AREA20-SUMMARY' direction 'in'",
]
output = conn.send_config_set(commands, exit_config_mode=False)
print("\nADD FILTER-LIST VIA VYOS:", output)

output = conn.commit()
print("COMMIT:", output)

output = conn.send_command_timing("save")
print("SAVE:", output)

output = conn.send_command_timing("exit")
print("EXIT:", output)

# Remove the extra area-type normal if it was added
out = conn.send_command("show configuration commands | grep 'area-type'", read_timeout=15)
print("\nAREA-TYPE config:", out)

# Clean up area-type normal if present (it's the default, shouldn't be there)
if "area-type normal" in out:
    commands = ["delete protocols ospf area 10 area-type"]
    output = conn.send_config_set(commands, exit_config_mode=False)
    print("DELETE AREA-TYPE:", output)
    output = conn.commit()
    print("COMMIT:", output)
    output = conn.send_command_timing("save")
    output = conn.send_command_timing("exit")

# Verify final config
out = conn.send_command("show configuration commands | grep ospf", read_timeout=15)
print("\nFINAL OSPF CONFIG:", out)

out = conn.send_command("show configuration commands | grep prefix-list", read_timeout=15)
print("\nFINAL PREFIX-LIST CONFIG:", out)

# Verify FRR
time.sleep(3)
out = conn.send_command("vtysh -c 'show running-config'", read_timeout=30)
print("\nFRR CONFIG:")
print(out)

conn.disconnect()
PYEOF

The instructions say "keep any scripts you write in the current directory," so the scripts stay. Now here is the final report.

---

## Report

### Faults Found

| # | Device | Fault | Design | Actual | Fix Commands |
|---|--------|-------|--------|--------|-------------|
| 1 | **Hub-A** | OSPF MD5 key case mismatch on eth0 | `LabArea0Key` | `LabArea0key` (lowercase k) | `delete protocols ospf interface eth0 authentication md5 key-id 1` then `set protocols ospf interface eth0 authentication md5 key-id 1 md5-key 'LabArea0Key'` + commit/save |
| 2 | **Hub-A** | Area 10 range wrong mask | `10.1.0.0/16` | `10.1.0.0/24` | `delete protocols ospf area 10 range 10.1.0.0/24` then `set protocols ospf area 10 range 10.1.0.0/16` + commit/save |
| 3 | **Hub-B** | Virtual-link peer uses IP instead of router-ID | `10.255.0.2` (Hub-A's RID) | `172.16.10.9` (Hub-A's eth3 address) | `delete protocols ospf area 10 virtual-link 172.16.10.9` then `set protocols ospf area 10 virtual-link 10.255.0.2 authentication md5 key-id 1 md5-key 'LabArea0Key'` + commit/save |
| 4 | **HQ-Edge** | BGP local-preference 200 on wrong ISP | ISP-A-IN gets 200 (prefer ISP-A) | ISP-B-IN had 200 (ISP-B preferred) | `delete policy route-map ISP-B-IN rule 10 set local-preference` then `set policy route-map ISP-A-IN rule 10 set local-preference 200` + commit/save |
| 5 | **HQ-Edge** | NAT rule 110 wrong outbound interface | eth2 (ISP-B link) | eth1 (same as rule 100) | `set nat source rule 110 outbound-interface name 'eth2'` + commit/save |
| 6 | **HQ-Edge** | OSPF default-information originate "always" | Conditional origination (only when HQ-Edge has a default itself) | `always` keyword present | `delete protocols ospf default-information originate always` then `set protocols ospf default-information originate` + commit/save |
| 7 | **Branch-2** | MTU 1400 on ether1 | Default 1500 | 1400 (caused ExStart with Hub-A) | `/interface ethernet set [find default-name=ether1] mtu=1500` |
| 8 | **Branch-2** | LAN OSPF template not passive | Passive (no hellos toward hosts) | Missing `passive` on 10.1.2.0/24 template | `/routing ospf interface-template set [find networks="10.1.2.0/24"] passive` |
| 9 | **Branch-3** | Extraneous firewall rule | No filtering (only Branch-4 filters) | `chain=forward action=drop protocol=ospf` | `/ip firewall filter remove *6` |
| 10 | **Branch-4** | Area 20 type default instead of stub | Stub (matches Hub-B's totally-stubby config) | `type=default` (mismatched stub flag, no adjacency with Hub-B) | `/routing ospf area set [find name=area20] type=stub` |
| 11 | **Branch-4** | Firewall rule 0 accepts all without connection-state | Stateful: accept only established,related | `action=accept` with no conditions (bypasses all drop rules) | Removed all rules, recreated: rule 0 `accept connection-state=established,related`, rule 1 `drop src=10.2.2.0/24 dst=10.0.0.0/8`, rule 2 `drop src=10.0.0.0/8 dst=10.2.2.0/24` |
| 12 | **B1-PC2** | Subnet mask /16 instead of /24 | `10.1.1.11/24` | `10.1.1.11/16` | `ip addr del 10.1.1.11/16 dev eth0; ip addr add 10.1.1.11/24 dev eth0; ip route add default via 10.1.1.1 dev eth0 onlink` + `sed -i` fix in `/etc/network/interfaces` |

**Additional fix (FRR bug workaround):** Hub-B's `area 20 range 10.2.0.0/16` was configured correctly per the design but FRR 10.5.1 did not suppress the component /24 Type-3 LSAs. Added `area 10 filter-list prefix AREA20-SUMMARY in` via vtysh with prefix-list denying 10.2.0.0/16 ge 17 and permitting all else. The prefix-list is saved in VyOS config; the filter-list is saved in frr.conf via `write memory`. VyOS's CLI does not support `area filter-list`, so this may not persist if VyOS regenerates FRR config on reboot.

### Verification

**1. Adjacencies and Sessions**

| Adjacency | State | Verified |
|-----------|-------|----------|
| HQ-Edge ↔ Hub-A (area 0) | Full | Yes |
| Hub-A ↔ Branch-1 (area 10) | Full | Yes |
| Hub-A ↔ Branch-2 (area 10) | Full | Yes |
| Hub-A ↔ Branch-3 (area 10) | Full | Yes |
| Branch-3 ↔ Hub-B (area 10) | Full | Yes |
| Hub-B ↔ Branch-4 (area 20, stub) | Full | Yes |
| Hub-A ↔ Hub-B (virtual link, area 0) | Full | Yes |
| eBGP ISP-A (203.0.113.1, AS 65100) | Established, 2 prefixes received, 0 sent | Yes |
| eBGP ISP-B (203.0.113.5, AS 65200) | Established, 2 prefixes received, 0 sent | Yes |

**2. Routing Tables**

| Check | Result |
|-------|--------|
| HQ-Edge default: BGP via ISP-A (203.0.113.1) preferred (locpref 200) | Yes |
| HQ-Edge backup default: ISP-B (203.0.113.5) present in BGP | Yes |
| HQ-Edge 8.8.8.8/32 via ISP-A, 1.1.1.1/32 via ISP-B | Yes |
| HQ-Edge advertises 0 routes to ISPs | Yes (PfxSnt=0) |
| HQ-Edge sees 10.1.0.0/16 and 10.2.0.0/16 only (no /24s) | Yes |
| All OSPF routers except HQ-Edge/Branch-4 have OSPF default | Yes |
| Branch-4 default from Hub-B stub injection | Yes |
| Branch-4 sees only default + 10.1.0.0/16 + area 20 locals + transit links | Yes |
| Area 10 routers see area 20 LANs only as 10.2.0.0/16 | Yes (after filter-list fix) |
| NAT: rule 100 on eth1, rule 110 on eth2 | Yes |

**3. Host Reachability**

| Test | Result |
|------|--------|
| Non-guest ↔ non-guest (56 pairs) | 56/56 PASS |
| Guest ↔ guest (2 pairs) | 2/2 PASS |
| Guest ↔ non-guest (32 pairs, should fail) | 32/32 correctly FAIL |
| All 10 hosts → 8.8.8.8 | 10/10 PASS |
| All 10 hosts → 1.1.1.1 | 10/10 PASS |

**4. Backup Path**

ISP-B default route present as BGP backup (locpref default 100 vs ISP-A's 200). All hosts can ping 1.1.1.1 (ISP-B loopback), confirming the ISP-B link and its NAT (rule 110 on eth2) work.

**5. Clean Config**

All fixes saved: VyOS `commit` + `save`, MikroTik changes immediate/persistent, Alpine `/etc/network/interfaces` updated. No diagnostic artifacts left on devices.

### Unresolved or Uncertain

- **Hub-B area filter-list persistence:** The `area 10 filter-list prefix AREA20-SUMMARY in` was needed to supplement `area 20 range 10.2.0.0/16` because FRR 10.5.1 does not suppress component Type-3 LSAs. VyOS's CLI doesn't support `area filter-list`, so it was applied via vtysh and saved to frr.conf. If VyOS regenerates frr.conf on reboot (before FRR loads it), the filter-list would be lost and the /24 routes would reappear in area 10. The area range configuration is correct per the design; this is an FRR platform limitation.
